nodes.title: Fitzgerald Family
nodes.content:
Joseph Fitzgerald was born December 31, 1869, in Sacramento, California. When Joseph was a little boy, he had a dog. Joseph liked the dog a lot and once when he thought the dog food was too hot, he got down to blow on it. The dog bit him. His dad was very upset and got out his gun to shoot the dog. The gun accidentally went off and shot his dad in the leg. The leg had to be amputated, eventually leading to gangrene and his dad’s death. Not sure what the fate of the dog was. 

Joseph shows up on the census living at an orphanage in Missoula when he was 10 years old. 

Katherine Calvin was born in 1872 in Kansas City, Kansas. Eventually she moved to Bearmouth with her family.

She met Joseph Fitzgerald in Bearmouth, and they got married in Butte in 1905. They moved to Garnet and rented a house there and hired Phil Newman, the local lumber mill owner, to build them a home up Dublin Gulch, where most of the Irish residence lived. Joseph and Catherine had three children, Mary, born in 1907, Margaret Anita, (who went by Anita) born in 1908 and Frank, born in 1912. 

A fire occurred several months after Frank was born which had a very large impact on their lives. 

The newspapers paper article reads: THE GRANITE COUNTY HERALD LATE EXTRA | OCTOBER 1912 GARNET IN ASHES! DEVASTATING BLAZE CONSUMES BUSINESS DISTRICT 

Flames Originate in Lyle & Fitzgerald Saloon; Only Handful of Structures Saved as Mining Camp Suffers Crushing Blow GARNET, MT — A catastrophic conflagration has swept through this mountain mining camp, leaving the once-proud business district in a state of utter ruin. The fire, which broke out late last night, reduced nearly half of the town’s commercial structures to smoldering ash and has dealt what many fear will be a permanent blow to this community.

According to local reports, the fire originated in the north side of town within the Lyle & Fitzgerald Saloon, located inside the Garnet Hotel. Fed by seasoned pine timbers and a lack of substantial foundations, the flames spread with terrifying speed. Because the town was built quickly during the gold rush of 1898, without coordination or an adequate water system, citizens were left virtually helpless against the advancing wall of fire. The entire north side of the main thoroughfare was quickly engulfed in flames. 

Out of all the properties on that side of the street, only the Adams Store remains standing. 

Heroic Efforts Save South Side Buildings 

As the fire threatened to leap across the dirt road and claim the remaining half of the town, local miners and merchants formed frantic bucket brigades. 

Thanks to the wide buffer of the main road, the intense efforts of the townspeople successfully spared several landmark businesses on the south side. Among those saved from destruction are: 

  • Davey’s General Store, operated by Frank A. Davey 
  • The Wells Hotel 
  • Kelly’s Bar

A Heavy Blow to a Declining Camp

While thankfully no fatalities have been reported, the financial ruin is severe. This disaster hits Garnet at an already vulnerable time. While the town boasted a peak population of nearly 1,000 residents at the turn of the century, recent years have seen gold veins wane and deeper shafts become too expensive to operate. The population had already dwindled to roughly 150 residents prior to the fire. With their livelihoods literally turned to ash, many of the remaining families are reportedly preparing to pack what little they have left and abandon the camp. 

Local merchant Frank A. Davey, however, has defiantly stated he intends to keep his store open for those miners who choose to stay and brave the winter. 

_____

After the fire, Joseph worked as a miner. 

The Fitzgerald family lived in Garnet until 1919 when they left, first to Hamilton, Montana and then to Yakima, Washington and eventually to Seattle, Washington. 

Frank graduated from high school in Yakima, Washington and then went to work in the theater in Seattle for a couple of years. 

He enlisted in the Navy right after Pearl Harbor and was stationed in San Francisco.

He was assigned to the USS Hale, a destroyer as a sonar operator for three years he served in the Pacific. After the war ended, he returned to the states and was discharged in 1945. 

Frank returned to Garnet in 1941. He went up to his house up Dublin Gulch, and there was a woman with children occupying it. He asked her to leave, but gave her a couple of weeks to do so. After World War II veterans could apply for a small land grant. Frank applied and was awarded 4 acres of land and the family cabin up Dublin Gulch, where their family home stood.

His sister Mary became a Catholic Nun, (Sister Mary Catherine of the Maryhurst Order). Anita, married Clarence Bohn but died of cancer at forty-eight. 

Joseph died in 1943 in Yakima and Catherine later married (Patrick Birmingham). 

She died in 1956, the same year as her daughter Anita.

Frank attended the University of Montana and graduated in 1950. He was a teacher at numerous schools in Nevada, Montana and Idaho, but for many years worked in Mullen, Idaho. He retired in 1975. 

He eventually moved back to Montana, purchasing a small home in Drummond and spending summers up Dublin Gulch in Garnet. He worked for many summers in the Garnet visitor center. He completed several interviews about Garnet residence and provided a lot of information regarding the town’s history. He was much loved. He died on St. Patrick’s Day in 2003 and is buried near his family’s cabin.

storyDetails.leadIn: Spanning from California orphanages to the historic ghost town of Garnet, Montana, the life of Joseph Fitzgerald and his family offer a vivid glimpse into the hardships and triumphs of early 20th-century frontier life.

nodes.title: Maud Markley
nodes.content:
Maud Markley grew up in a tough part of Missoula, at the edge of the red-light District
on Front Street. Her father was deceased, and her mother lived with Maud’s stepfather,
known to be a violent man.

When Maud was seventeen, Mrs. F.H. Nickey accused her of stealing a 15-yard bolt of
white satin, one white lace overdress, one rose, colored silk purse, and one silk
handkerchief. Two witnesses saw Maud attempt to hide these items, and one testified
that Maud had admitted to the crime and wanted to give the material back to Mrs.
Nickey. Instead, she was arrested and taken before justice of the peace W.J. Myers.

She pled not guilty. The witnesses testified and bond was set at $40, the estimated
value of the stolen goods. Maud’s mother and stepfather did not show up for the
hearing.

Since Maud, the defendant did not have the bond money, she was sent to jail. Justice of
the Peace Meyers remanded the case to judge Frank Woody, who listened to the same
testimony, heard Maud’s plea of not guilty and proceeded to sentence her to the state
reform school at Miles city to serve time until she was twenty-one years old. Two and a
half years later, when Maud was 19, she was released early from the reform school and
placed on parole.

On January 25,1899, she found herself in Connors and Hardwood salon in Garnet. It
was not common for women, especially young, single females, to be in the saloons. The
drinking turned heavy and Maud was a center of attention.

At about 2 AM, someone summon Thomas Maguire into the street. Several witnesses
watch the next series of events, but nobody interfered to put an end to it.

Daniel McPherson, Jack Lavelle, Mike Lavelle, and Joe Irwin proceeded to beat, kick, and stab
Thomas McGuire. McGuire suffered from the total of eight stabs, with the most serious
one directly over the kidneys. Constable John Elkins, and justice of the peace Childs
were woken up and told about the crime.

The four men were charged with the crime of assault within intent to kill, and warrants
were issued for their arrest. Though McGuire’s condition was serious, his doctor
believed that the victim would recover as long as he did not experience, unforeseen
complications.

After all legal proceedings, and all was said and done, Markley received the brunt of the
punishment for the night of the crime, whereas the clear culprits were released.

A few weeks after the incident, Maud Markley was ordered back to the state reform school for
15 months. By March of that year, the charges against Daniel McPherson and Mike
Lavelle were dismissed. At their trial, Joe Irwin and Jack Lavelle were found not guilty.

In the newspaper report of the incident, editor Cole’s tone towards Maud is that she was
the cause of the commotion he said, “As usual it is said that the whole row occurred
over one of those ‘commercial fairies’, and this time it was a very young girl who had
formally resided in Missoula, and who is currently being paroled from the reformed
school at Miles City.”

In a later comment about the incident, Cole says, “This is the same piece of tough
femininity that caused all the trouble in Garnet recently, whereas four men are now in
jail, and another severely injured.”

Seemingly, to dismiss Joe Irwin‘s actions by noting
the civility of his family, editor Cole gave a warm account of a social gathering that read
as follows: There was a pleasant

party at the hospital home of Mr. and Mrs. Joel Irwin Senior Tuesday evening. There
was singing and splendid music by the mandolin club, after which there was a dainty
luncheon. The house was full and everyone had a good time.” The Irwin’s were a very
popular family in Garnet, with both Joseph Senior and his son Joe employed as minors.
The Irwin’s daughter, Virginia was one of the most popular women of marrying age in
town. Social gatherings at the Irwin’s house were given detailed coverage in the Garnet
Mining News.

The surviving accounts cannot tell us with certainty whether social standing directly
influenced the legal decisions. However, the different ways Maud and the Irwin family
were portrayed—and the fact that Maud was returned to reform school while the men
involved in the assault ultimately escaped conviction—raise an important question about
how gender, reputation, family standing, and social status may have influenced the way
justice was administered in mining towns at the end of the nineteenth century.

storyDetails.leadIn:
Maud Markley’s story offers a glimpse into the difficult lives of young women on
the margins of society—and raises questions about how justice was applied
depending on social status.

nodes.title: Ole and Marian Dahl Garnet, Montana
Ole and Marian Dahl Garnet, Montana
nodes.content:
John "Ole" Dahl and Marian Dahl. Ole was born in Norway and immigrated to the USA at the
age of 19. He spoke with a Norwegian accent his whole life. He married Marian when she was
16 years and he was 33. They had three children, John Raymond, Marjorie and Jay. The Dahl
family moved to Garnet in 1933, after selling a bus business that Ole operated.

The family first lived in one of the small cabins up on the hillside behind the hotel, then moved
to a house up Dublin Gulch, (probably the Wells house) then to the Hanifen house before
moving into what is now called the Dahl Cabin.

Marian & Ole bought a gas-powered washing machine that was delivered up to Garnet to
someone who couldn’t afford it. Marian said of that machine, “God, I was tickled to death, my
rubbing days are over.”

Her daughter Maggie commented, “You could hear it all over Garnet.” Eventually, the Dahls
installed an electric light generator in a shed and ran power to the house.

Their son John served in the army during World War 11. At the age of 41, he was cleaning his
gun in the kitchen of the family home in Garnet when the weapon discharged. He lived about
45 minutes. He was preparing to go hunting Monday morning.

The Dahls made their own home brew beer and had a man cap the bottles. One day it was too
warm and the caps popped off. They had to drink all the beer before it went bad. About 1938,
Ole opened a new saloon at the site of Charlie Davis’s old saloon. His daughter said that Ole
“borrowed $50 to build ‘The Joint.’” This is now the Visitor’s Center.

Ole’s memory got bad and one day he got lost coming back up the mountain. He spent a cold
night out before he was discovered. They moved to Anaconda where Ole died on his 83 rd
birthday. Marian moved to Fife, Washington area to live with her daughter for several years.

storyDetails.leadIn:
John “Ole” and Marian Dahl arrived in Garnet in 1933 and built a life there that captures the
resourcefulness, hardships, and colorful everyday experiences of the families who called
Garnet home in its later years.
storyDetails.sourceLabel: Credits go to the book ‘The Road to Garnet Gold’, a brief history of Montana’s gold rush, feature one of the last Ghost Towns compiled by the Bureau of Land Management.

nodes.title: Chinese
nodes.content:
Ah Chung, Ah Chung, Ah Pew, Ah Lou, Ah Look, Ah Sue, Ah Gee, Ah Lee, Ah For, Ah
Shue, Ah Shee, Ah Moon and Ah Young are all names that show up on the census
records from Garnet, but very little is known about them.

The Chinese arrived in Montana as early as the 1860s. The war-wracked Kwangtung,
province, a coastal region of China, had been the home to many the Chinese who
ended up on the Montana mining frontier. That war and the lack of American workers on
the western mining landscape set the stage for Chinese immigrants.

The Chinese tended to move into mining camps after the initial rush had died down.
However, in Beartown, a man named Gee Lee, was with the town from its beginning.
After trying mining, he decided laundering was more profitable and established Gee
Lee’s washhouse, which was one of the cornerstones of the town.

Another notable Chinese man in Beartown was called one eyed Tom. Tom would trek
into the mountains each fall to gather herbs, which he stored in his cabin and used them
to aid the injured or ill people of the town.

Racism against the Chinese was virulent throughout all of Montana territory, especially
in the mining camps. For a time, the whites tolerated the Chinese as long as they stuck
to working what was considered menial jobs, such as servants, or laundry.
Garnet did have a Chinese laundry.

When engaged in mining, they usually worked in small groups away from the white
miners. They were at times, segregated to living in special districts, which was likely the
case in Garnet. During the decade of the 1880s, the Chinese endured a wave of hatred
and discrimination throughout the nation.

Congress passed the Chinese exclusion act in 1882, which put a 10-year moratorium
on the importation of Chinese labor and prohibited Chinese immigrants from becoming
US citizens.

In 1892 the law was extended for 10 years, and by 1902, it became permanent.

Chinese burials were kept secret, as rumor suggested Chinese miners buried their gold
with them, and graves were often desecrated.

storyDetails.leadIn:
The story of Garnet includes people from many backgrounds, including a small
but largely forgotten Chinese community whose names remain in the town’s
census records.

nodes.title: Sam Ritchey
nodes.content:
Samuel Ritchey was born on August 16, 1833 on a farm located 20 miles from what would
become the city of Chicago, Illinois. By his 18th birthday, he had, by his own admission, caught
“the gold fever and never got cured.”
In 1852, him and his brother left Home with four-yoke steers, some horses and a wagon and
worked their way west through hostile Indian country arriving in Jackson County, Oregon by
September. Eventually, Sam and his brother sold their livestock and wagon and began
prospecting. Sam mined, packed and traded horses in that area during ensuring years until
1862.
Sam moved to the mining camps of Elk Creek in Montana, where he set up a butchering
business that he operated until July 1867. He traveled to other mining areas and returned in
1873 to Montana to begin prospecting in the area that would become Garnet. In 1874 he
stumbled across a piece of quartz that look promisingly. He named the mine ‘the Nancy Hanks’
after Abraham Lincoln’s mother. Twenty-two years later the Nancy Hanks would make Sam
Ritchey a wealthy man at the age of 63 and spur the development of the town of Garnet.
It’s uncertain how much wealth Sam accumulated while living in Garnet. In his autobiography
Gold Fever, he proclaimed the following. “I worked in the Garnet district for twenty-six years
before I sold any ore and I am still digging the ground of ore. I struck ore in the Nancy Hanks
mine in 1896. In 1897, 1898 and 1899 I took out $550,000 in gold and silver from the Nancy
Hanks, Cascade and Spokane mines. Since that time, I have leased some ground, which has
produced about $150,000.”
Montana Historian Dan Cushman calculated that, considering the ore value and the amount
shipped to the smelter in Anaconda, Sam Ritchey and his partner big Jim Auchinvole were
realizing ‘about $7,500 per week.” Today’s value (2026) that would be $1,606,500 per week,
making Sam Ritchey one if not, they’ve wealthiest mine owner in the county.
Sam Ritchey was a bachelor in his mining days. In 1900 he sold the Nancy Hanks mine. He was
67 years old and ready to begin a new chapter.

Sam Ritchey cut a dashing figure, even at the age of 67. He was handsome, wealthy and, from
all accounts, well liked and admire for his business skills. During 1900 he made many trips to
visit an old friend and a former prospector George W Morse, who had a ranch near the small
community of New Chicago, located a few miles south of Drummond. Richie had a long
connection with the town, having owned a billiard hall there as early as 1877.
Now, however the business he was attending to in New Chicago was strictly personal. George
Morris had made his fortune and could afford to hire a servant. Her name was Lena Stai, she
was in her early twenties, and Sam Ritchey had fallen in love with her. Lena came from
Minnesota, born to parents originally from Norway. Lena venture to Montana after seeing an
advertisement in her local newspaper requesting “a girl to work on a big cattle ranch near
Drummond, Montana”.
Sam Ritchey, who took his young fiancé to the big city of Butte to tie the knot. An article in the
Anaconda Standard in November 1900 commented on the event:
Samuel Ritchey, a well-known mining man from Garnet, and Granite County came to Butte a
few days ago and last evening was married to Miss Lena Stai, a young lady of this city. Judge
William Clancy performed the ceremony. Mr. Ritchey has been a bachelor, and, according to the
marriage record, he heroically admits to being 67 years of age, while his bride is but 21. Mr. and
Mrs. Ritchey left for the south on a wedding trip and expect to be away for about five months,
much of the time will be spent in Arkansas Hot Springs. Mr. Ritchey is the owner of the Nancy
Hanks Mine in Garnet and other mining properties and is reputed to be a very wealthy man.
When the Ritchey’s return to Garnet, Sam had the finest house in town to domicile with his
new bride. With a wide porch, extending across the front, the carefully crafted log house
located near the Nancy Hanks Mine befitted a man of Sam Rictcheys position in the community.
As one entered the parlor to the left of the main entrance, Lena Ritchey’s piano came into view.
Continuing into the living room, a large room was made comfortable with fine furniture,
including a couch, rocking chair, bookshelf, straight back chairs, tables, and the latest of family
entertainment inventions, a phonograph. Next to the living room, a dining area contained a
beautiful table, chairs, a china closet and a stylish area rug, an amenity that also appeared in
the parlor and dining room. In contrast to most of the homes in Garnet, the walls and ceilings of
all three rooms were papered, and each room had its own heater.
A spacious kitchen made up the rear portion of the house and contained a large cooking range,
cupboards, tables, and a sink. A small room next to the kitchen contain a wooden bathtub and
received water (to be heated on the kitchen range) piped into from a reservoir. Leaving the
house from the kitchen, one was protected from the elements by a covered passageway that
led uphill to the outhouse and the woodshed. The comfortable two-story house had his own

bedrooms upstairs. Outside, at some distance from the house, stood a large stable for the
horses and an adjacent structure to store carriages and wagons.
Sam and Lena Richie soon started a family. Helene E. Ritchey was born October 6, 1903, and
Samuel Ritchey Junior arrived the following year. Both of the children attended school in
Garnet through the eighth grade and then continued their education in Missoula.

storyPhotos.caption: he Ritchey family home in Garnet, with its broad covered porch and log railings.

storyDetails.leadIn:
Samuel Ritchey was a 19th-century gold prospector whose discovery of the legendary Nancy
Hanks Mine transformed him into one of Montana's wealthiest mining figures and sparked
the rise of the historic boomtown of Garnet.

nodes.title: Winifred and JK Wells
nodes.content:
During late 1897 and early 1898, Winifred Wells over saw the construction of the Wells Hotel, a 40-by-50-foot, two- and one-half story building that stands on Garnet Ghost Town’s Main Street today. As newlyweds John Kay Wells and Winifred moved to Beartown, started a family, and became successful business people. John operated a butcher shop and initiated the building of the first school there. In 1896, the family moved to Garnet.

Winifred Wells designed the elegant new hotel in Garnet with elaborate detail trim inside and out. This included ornate moldings, stained glass in the front door inserts, and in a circular window located high under the front gable. It also had a solid oak staircase, with turned spindles—and perhaps the most appreciated feature, skylights on the top floor – so the minors who slept up there at a reduced rate, on the floor in their bedrolls, could stare up at the stars, after spending a hard day in the dark, wet tunnels of the mines.

The Wells hotel immediately became Garnet’s premier, accommodation, and eating place. It’s grand opening was truly historic a reporter in the Bear Mountain News:

“Great things are expected when it was announced that JK Wells would soon open his hotel with a grand ball on 17 March, but even those who expected the most, we’re agreeably surprised from the moment they entered the front door and till the last strains of music died away at 7 o’clock next morning…  Mr. and Mrs. Wells waited in person on the tables and took special care that no-one was overlooked. Supper was served to 180 people.”

The March 24, 1898 issue of the Bear Mountain news elaborated on the Wells opening calling it “the best dance ever given in Garnet.” the article also reported that “Butte, Anaconda, Deer Lodge, Drummond and Missoula, and all the neighboring towns were represented.” The extensive construction activity that occurred in the new town of Garnet between 1897 and 98 marked the beginning of Garnets preeminence as a center of mining activity in the area. By 1899, the Nancy Hanks was employing two shifts of 12 miners who kept busy blasting a shaft down to the 100-foot level. Blasting, individual mine whistles, and construction noise changed the atmosphere of the formally quiet mountain town into a cacophony of progress. Most of the miners around Garnet lived within 1 mile of town.

storyDetails.leadIn: Winifred Wells played a pivotal role in shaping the social and architectural landscape of Garnet, Montana, during its late 19th-century mining boom

nodes.title: John H. Toole
nodes.content:
John H. Toole was born in Missoula in 1919 and grew up there, though for a time the Toole family also had a home up Dublin Gulch. “Johnny,” as he was called, spent his teenage years working his family’s mines in the Douglas Creek and Top O’Deep area and in Garnet.

He played accordion and guitar in a band that often performed in Garnet in the 1930s, alongside fiddle and banjo players. They played ragtime, jazz, waltzes, polkas, and schottisches. Toole described the scene in the bar around midnight:

Many (in the bar) were veterans of World War I. It became a ritual that, at midnight, we would play “My Buddy,” the poignant song of death in the trenches sixteen years before. Everybody would rise, heads bowed, and silently gaze at the floor. The song would end; a miner would boom out, “Parlez vous!” and we would launch into the rollicking “Mademoiselle from Armentières.” The miners would sail across the floor yelling Hi-Yee Hi-Yee Hi-Yee! and the old hall would begin to shake and sway again. Was there an economic collapse in America? At this moment of the blending of rhythm, music and pure mountain air, these superbly strong people were happily unaware of it.

— John H. Toole

By 1936, Garnet had changed. Toole was visiting the Circle W, a dude ranch owned by the Weisel family, when the guests decided to see the “ghost town” of Garnet. John Weisel and Toole drove a Model A Ford over the rough old mining road from Greenough Hill past Coloma and down into Garnet to scout the trip before the guests followed. Toole described that visit:

Garnet was beginning a new relapse into a long sleep. Upon our entry into town, Mr. Davey came out in the street and greeted us, but the throng of miners had diminished; the mines had proved to be poorer than anticipated and jobs were more plentiful in the county. Nevertheless, I rounded up some musicians for a dance, and in a couple of days the Weisel pack string and guests arrived. There was the usual exploration of the old buildings, the fruitless efforts involved in panning for gold and ‘oohing’ and ‘ahhing’ over Mr. Davey’s inventory. In 1936 this inventory was Garnet’s most intriguing attraction.

— John H. Toole

storyDetails.leadIn: As a teenager in the 1930s, John “Johnny” Toole saw Garnet change from a bustling mining town into the quiet place it would become.

nodes.title: The Seadin Family
nodes.content:
Nels and Lena Seadin were Swedish immigrants who came to Garnet in 1905. Nels was a miner, and over the years the family moved away from Garnet many times, following work. In 1930 they returned for the last time, and Nels served as Garnet’s postmaster until his death in 1939.

Tor Seadin

Tor, the Seadins’ son, was born in Garnet and graduated from high school in Missoula. In 1923 he enrolled at the School of Mines in Butte, which specialized in science and engineering. He spent the summer before classes began working at the Elm Orlu mine in Butte, where he was killed in a mine explosion.

Margaret Seadin

Margaret, the Seadins’ daughter, was also born in Garnet. She was born with spina bifida and used a wheelchair throughout her life. With her bouncing blonde curls, she was adored by the whole town. She died of complications of her condition at 25.

storyDetails.leadIn: The Seadin family was among the many immigrant families who came to Garnet seeking opportunity and made their lives in this remote mining town.
storyDetails.sourceLabel: Family information and photos courtesy of Sharon Seadin Baldwin, granddaughter of Nels and Lena Seadin

nodes.title: Samuel and Jennie Adams
nodes.content:
Samuel Adams came west from Pennsylvania with his friend Pete Shipler to seek his fortune in Montana. He bought and opened the Adams Mercantile and partnered with Shipler in mining at Copper Cliff and other locations. In 1904, Samuel returned to Pennsylvania and married Jennie Starr.

After a short time in Missoula, the couple settled in Garnet. Thanks to Samuel’s mining interests and other ventures, the Adams house was considered one of the nicest homes in town, second only to the more elegant Sam Ritchie home. It stood at the top of the hill above town: a three-room log house covered in yellow drop siding, with a white picket fence and an organ and plants in the parlor. Jennie Adams served as Garnet’s postmistress in the early 1900s.

The family knew loss. Their son Samuel Jr. was born and died in 1906. Their daughter Mary Agnes was born in 1909 and lived until 1912. Mary Jane Adams was born on March 2, 1917, at St. Patrick’s Hospital in Missoula.

Mary Jane remembered Christmas in Garnet as a special treat. Her father trimmed the tree with candles clipped to the ends of the branches, lighting two or three so she could see them before putting them out because of the fire danger. Strings of popcorn finished the decorations. She also remembered picnics at Warren Park and the gardens the family grew.

The Adams family lived in Garnet from 1904 to 1927, moving to Missoula when Mary Jane was 10. She married Alan Morin, raised two sons, and ran a boarding house in Missoula, where Garnet’s blacksmith, Billie Liberty, was one of her boarders. Starting in the 1940s, she returned to spend many summer days in Garnet, and for years she came up for Garnet Appreciation Day, where she was well known and well liked.

storyDetails.leadIn: The Adams family’s story is one of prosperity, success, and the kind of sadness felt by many mining families in Garnet.

nodes.title: Edward Brook Warren
nodes.content:
Edward Brook Warren was born on February 2, 1861, in Ontario, Canada, and came to the United States in 1882. He settled in Butte, married, and ran a boarding house with his wife. After a divorce, he moved to Garnet.

In October 1898, the Butte Daily Post reported on his change of fortune:

As a Life Insurance Agent, He Was a Failure, but as a Prospector, He Is About to Realize on His Stock of Energy—Struck It Rich Near Garnet.

Edward B. Warren has encountered a body of rich free milling gold ore in one of his claims near Garnet, and no one who knows him will be sorry to hear of his good fortune. Mr. Warren was formerly a resident of Butte. While here, he has followed two occupations, that of life insurance agent and salesman in a shoe store, but in neither following did he acquire a sufficient amount of worlds goods to enable him to rest comfortably on Easy Street the balance of his days.

Last January he concluded that telling a man how much money he would have coming to him after he died was not the business for which he had been created and, like a race horse going over the first hurtle, he leaped the job and struck out for Garnet with nothing on which to operate save a prospector’s pick, a shoemaker’s last and a bottomless shaft of pluck.

On arriving at his destination, he opened a shoe store, but about the time ‘things began to come his way’ the place caught fire and burned down. All of his stock of shoes was destroyed, as was also the last, but the pick and his pluck were saved. With these he began to prospect and in a short time had located several claims he considered good. On July 4, he discovered the one on which he made the strike. In view of the fact it was found on the Nation’s Day, he called it the National. Ben Mount, a well-known mining man of that section, has an interest in the property. The vein is about several feet in width and has every appearance of being a true fissure of the high-pressure brand. Liberal offers have already been made for the property by men of means, but there is no prospect of a sale just now.

— Butte Daily Post, October 6, 1898

Warren’s cabin was tucked into the forest a little over a mile from town, toward the north side of the mountain range.

storyDetails.leadIn: A life defined by perseverance, community, and the thrill of discovery: Edward Warren went from a struggling Butte salesman to one of Garnet’s most cherished miners and residents.

nodes.title: Kelly’s Saloon and Residence
nodes.content:
Kelly’s Saloon is a two-story, false-front building on Garnet’s Main Street. Built before the 1898 gold boom, it was originally known as the Bob Moore Saloon. In October 1898, L.P. Kelly bought it from Robert Moore for $1,500. After Kelly sold a partial interest, it became the Kelly and Fraser Saloon.

The Kelly family lived in the apartment above the saloon. It had two bedrooms and one large room with a kitchen range, cupboards, a table and chairs, a couch, and several rocking chairs.

Garnet’s saloons were for men; women and children rarely went inside. So visitors calling on Mrs. Kelly announced themselves at the outside staircase and climbed the stairs to her apartment.

Frank Fitzgerald, a longtime Garnet resident, remembered visiting Mrs. Kelly with his mother when he was a small boy, and being served a glass of beer.

During Prohibition, the entire building became the family’s home. The Kellys left Garnet in the 1930s. The building has been the focus of extensive preservation work over the years, and descendants of the Kelly family return to Garnet and take part in Garnet Day activities.

storyDetails.leadIn: Kelly’s Saloon offers a rare look at how a saloon owner’s family lived in late-19th-century Garnet.
storyDetails.voiceQuote: I can remember holding this big glass, it seemed big to me. My hands wouldn’t go all the way around it and I can remember drinking that beer and I like beer pretty well and I can remember that real well, ’cause I know I spilled some of the beer and was kidded about being drunk.

nodes.title: Philip Neuman
nodes.content:
Philip Neuman was born in Buffalo, New York, in 1864 and arrived in the Garnet area in his early thirties. He owned a large steam-powered sawmill on Anderson Hill, near Garnet, that supplied lumber for the town’s buildings, mines, and mills.

Philip fell in love with a woman from a red-light district and set out to build her a home. Townsfolk called it the “Gingerbread House.” No detail of its design or construction was too small. He hauled a piano up the steep grade and bought a new Majestic range from the Missoula Mercantile so his bride would have every luxury.

Before the house was finished, she took the stage to Helena and never returned. Philip stopped construction and lived alone in the unfinished house. He died of influenza in Philipsburg at the age of 56.

Philip also built the Joseph Fitzgerald house up Dublin Gulch, the only house in Garnet with a concrete foundation, and a showcase of his design and craftsmanship. The Gingerbread House was destroyed by arson in 1971.

storyDetails.leadIn: Philip Neuman’s story is one of love, craftsmanship, and heartbreak, and the unfinished house he left behind became known as Garnet’s “Gingerbread House.”
storyDetails.sourceLabel: BLM, The Road to Garnet’s Gold

nodes.title: John Leshou
nodes.content:
John Leshou was born in Holstein, Germany, in 1840. Like many of his countrymen, he left to escape ongoing war, most likely sailing from Hamburg, and eventually settled in Iowa, home to a large German community.

He worked as a bullwhacker, driving ox teams, and was eventually asked to bring a team of oxen and supplies west to Montana’s Bitterroot Valley on the Bozeman Trail. The route earned the name “Bloody Bozeman”: it cut through the territory of the Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho, who fought to defend it, and many travelers died along the way. The survivors reached Fort Owen in the Bitterroot Valley.

Prospectors passing through spoke of gold on Bear Creek, a two-day ride away. Leshou made his way to Beartown, where he opened a trading post and served as postmaster. He and his friend Charles Kroger were invited to dinner in Deer Lodge to meet two sisters from his hometown in Holstein. In 1873, John married Dora Rusch, and Charles married her sister. John and Dora raised their three children in Beartown.

Leshou and Kroger decided to mine farther up the gulch, in the area that would become Garnet. They bought a claim in 1873, the first claim surveyed in the headwaters of what became the Garnet district. They found gold: according to geologist J.T. Pardee, the claim yielded $240,000.

In 1892, John began buying hundreds of acres of land along Grant Creek, along with water rights. In 1900 he became president of the Western Montana National Bank on Higgins Street in Missoula. He died in 1921, and he and Dora are buried in the Missoula Cemetery. Several miners are buried near them; it is said John paid for their burials when their luck didn’t pan out.

storyPhotos.caption: John Leshou with his granddaughter Dora.

storyDetails.leadIn: John Leshou left a war-torn homeland, crossed the “Bloody Bozeman” Trail, and built a fortune in the Garnet mining district.
